subtitulo: The five short moves that open a shop, clear a doorway and close an exchange well
cena: The shopkeeper's eyes are already on the shelf you're about to touch, and the five seconds before you touch it are the whole lesson.

steps.pt: Politeness here is timing, not sentences: greet before you look, con permiso before you move, gracias before you go.

steps.promptPt: You open the door of a small shop in the morning. Before looking at the shelves, greet the person at the counter. Speak now.

steps.pt: Good morning. How can I help?
Dígame just means the floor is yours — not a request for your life story. If you're browsing, just say so.

steps.promptPt: The shopkeeper asks how she can help, but you only want to look. Say that, and thank her. Speak now.

steps.pt: Crowded lift, narrow aisle, blocked doorway: say con permiso before you squeeze through — announcing the move, not apologising.

steps.promptPt: The lift doors open and one person is standing across the exit. Ask permission before moving past. Speak now.
They make room and say pásele. Thank them as you pass. Speak now.

steps.pt: Last move: hasta luego doesn't promise a return — it's just the ordinary sign-off leaving a shop or counter.

steps.promptPt: You have paid at a taquería and are walking out. Thank them and sign off before the door closes. Speak now.
steps.pt: Thank you very much. See you.
Take care; hope it goes well.

steps.promptPt: They answer que le vaya bien. Return the wish with one word. Speak now.

steps.pt: B02 complete. Buenos días first, con permiso before you move, gracias and hasta luego on the way out.

aprofundar.titulo: Short courtesy, placed at the right moment

secoes.corpo: You do not need to produce either word in B02. Dígame opens your turn at a counter. Pásele grants passage or invites you in. Recognising them prevents the pause that makes a simple courtesy feel complicated.

exemplos.pt: Go ahead; how can I help?

secoes.corpo: In Mexico, ¿mande? can answer a call or replace a sharp ¿qué? when someone was not heard. The visitor may simply recognise it; producing it is optional. The Academia Mexicana de la Lengua describes it as a courtesy marker, not proof of colonial submission.
Use con permiso before crossing physical space. Use perdón when you have actually bumped into somebody or made a mistake. Keeping those jobs separate makes both phrases clearer.

permissao: You are allowed to say almost nothing and still land it. Buenos días, con permiso, gracias, hasta luego — four short pieces, always placed a beat earlier than an English speaker's instinct. You do not need pásele, dígame or ¿mande? in your own mouth; recognising them when they come back is the whole ask.
espelho: In English, 'excuse me' does double duty for both moving past someone and apologising for a mistake, so the two feel like one habit. In Mexico they are two different words doing two different jobs — con permiso announces a movement before it happens, perdón repairs one that already went wrong — and collapsing them into a single all-purpose 'sorry' is the tell that gives an English speaker away.
frasePiso: Greet before the request, ask permission before the body moves, and sign off before the door closes.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You walk into a small shop and go straight to the shelf you want, and the attendant's face cools slightly before you have said a single word.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: She doesn't want to help me, or shopkeepers here are just less friendly than at home.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: In Mexico the greeting is the opening move of the transaction, not decoration around it. Walking straight to the merchandise skips the one word that tells the room you are a person and not just a customer, and that omission reads as the discourtesy, not your accent.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say buenos días or buenas tardes to the room on the way in, before you look at anything.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The same attendant who cooled off a second earlier turns attentive, because you have just done the one thing that opens the exchange properly.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a large supermarket or chain store with no single attendant to greet — the courtesy is about entering a space someone is actively minding, not a rule for every doorway in the country.
